title: The Galatian sickness and why only Christ saves
english: Once the preaching had been received among the Gentiles, some men coming from the circumcision began persuading the Gentiles to live as Jews, and the first dispute about this matter seems to have arisen in Antioch, for the apostles wrote that believers should not be subject to the law but should abstain from food offered to idols and from blood and from what is strangled and from sexual immorality, for so it seemed good to the Holy Spirit.

This sickness took hold of the Galatians, since they joined together in wanting to live as Jews, and they were persuaded by men who distort the truth and claim that the other apostles do not stop anyone who wishes to keep the law.
Severianus says Paul shows that neither Moses died for the world nor any other of the prophets, so we must not be mastered by one who did not save us but by Him who died for us.
Paul says, “to another gospel, which is not another” (Galatians 1:6-7), for our gospel and the gospel of the apostles want you to be outside the law.

Severianus asks, granted an angel, why does Paul also say 'we'? Paul means: when we preached we preached by the power of the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit does not change His mind, so if we say anything different we have abandoned the things of the Spirit, and therefore let the preacher who sets aside the preaching be accursed.

Paul says, “what you received” (Galatians 1:9), and Severianus explains his meaning: it is not that I preached and you did not receive, but I did preach and you did receive, and just as I do not regret having preached, so you must hold fast to what you received.

Paul asks, “Am I now persuading men or God, or am I seeking to please men, for if I still pleased men I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10), and Severianus says Paul is about to remind them of his own gospel, so he first secures his position so they will not think he flatters them by yielding, for he rebukes them while he exhorts them, and by saying “still” he revealed that he once pleased men, and whom did he please but those from whom he received letters to harm the believers in Damascus, so Paul says, if I still pleased the Jews I would not have believed in Christ.

Severianus asks why Paul mentions his former life in Judaism except to show that he serves not from prejudice but in truth, for it was not because he hated the law that he fled to grace, since he had even avenged the law, but because he found what is perfect he left the law behind, and now Paul shows that he has something more than those around Peter, for they never showed zeal for Judaism by opposing Christianity as he did, so Paul says, do not think I came to grace because I hated the law, for I had avenged the law, but I found what is perfect, and I do not equate the law with perfect grace.
Severianus says Paul speaks not to slander the apostles but to declare that he did not follow mortal flesh.

Severianus says Paul argues that if no one of those who bear the toil is justified by works but one is justified by faith, where ease is found and the greatness of righteousness, then how is it not necessary to leave the law behind and be content with grace, for when Paul says no one can be justified by works of the law he means works, not commandments, since a commandment justifies when it is heard, whereas the work was what was hard to accomplish.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in epistulam ad Galatas u01-open
orientation: Severianus explains how some from the circumcision persuaded Gentile believers to live as Jews, and Paul answers by defending grace against law keeping.
